Consider Silver Star as a warrior.

What makes one person into a great disaster is her power of mental contamination. ...That is not our concern just now.

What makes that person the strongest, first of all, is gravitational flight. That is our concern.

Ordinarily, a warrior gets thrust from the <ruby>Gattari<rt>gattari</rt></ruby>—the <ruby>wing tubes<rt>barrels</rt></ruby>—and lift from the <ruby>horo<rt>horo</rt></ruby>—the <ruby>wing armor<rt>wings</rt></ruby>. Thus flight, or <ruby>armored flight<rt>Nail</rt></ruby>, becomes possible.

Nothing else in humanity's possession travels faster.

Faster than every vehicle, every ship, every airship: that makes a warrior the absolute owner of the choice to engage. He decides whether there will be a fight. Moreover, bodily attacks are his main weapon, so speed becomes destructive force, sufficient to inflict fatal damage on any weapon.

For these reasons, warriors stand above all other arms. Kings of the battlefield.

Silver Star is king among warriors for much the same reason.

An ordinary warrior uses Gattari and horo to manipulate the <ruby>air<rt>wind</rt></ruby> and fly. Silver Star asks no more than a supporting role of air. Remove the air, and she can still <ruby>fly<rt>fly</rt></ruby>.

Those thin, faintly shining, fragile wings entrust themselves not to air but to <ruby>celestial force<rt>shinki</rt></ruby>—gravity, universal attraction.

One of nature's most fundamental <ruby>forces<rt>energies</rt></ruby>.

Silver Star. Second Generation Uemon-no-jou Muramasa recognizes, grasps and controls this force. The gravity arising from surrounding objects and from her own body—within the limit of her pilot's <ruby>heat output<rt>power</rt></ruby>, she increases it, reduces it, or changes the direction in which it acts.

Gravitational flight, founded on this principle, reaches an entirely different plane from ordinary flight.

The higher warrior had Earth's gravity on his side and charged with greater force. For the lower warrior it was the reverse: gravity opposed him, and he intercepted while losing force.

How great the difference became depended on the angle.

Roughly, the higher warrior's angle of descent and the lower warrior's angle of ascent could be considered directly proportional. Move that angle away from ninety degrees, and the gap in force diminished. Bring it toward ninety, and the gap opened, multiplying.

And at present the angle was <ruby>almost ninety degrees<rt>・・・・・</rt></ruby>.

Eighty-nine, perhaps. Horizontal distance and difference in altitude gave us this result.

Not bad.

Silver Star in perfect condition would surely have made it eighty-nine point nine.

I chose to forget the expression about a drop in the bucket.

...Whichever way one put it, nearly ninety degrees.

The enemy would race almost vertically down. We would race almost vertically up. That much was settled.

Silver Star would come from the stratosphere, enjoying gravity's fullest assistance and increasing it further with her own ability.

Momentum equals mass times velocity. What figure would that produce?

...I abandoned the calculation halfway. Not because I had discovered enough energy to stack at least twenty Muramasas together and <ruby>break them like roof tiles<rt>・・・</rt></ruby>, and had lost heart. No.

Finding the answer served no purpose to begin with.

Enough energy to break the enemy's armor was enough. Anything beyond it, one could safely call waste. Smash the armor beyond recognition, or open the carotid artery with a neck cut of a few inches—the value was the same.

On that count, going against gravity, we could hardly obtain the necessary energy by ourselves.

But collision force, naturally, was decided <ruby>relatively<rt>・・・</rt></ruby>.

If Silver Star's dive carried enough collision force to destroy us, our <ruby>counterstroke<rt>counter</rt></ruby> would receive the same force. So the reasoning went.

The enemy could destroy us. We could destroy the enemy.

...Equal, then? Not at all.

Altitude divided advantage from disadvantage. Common knowledge in warrior combat, and being common knowledge, it left no room for doubt.

Two lumps of iron colliding—there, above or below would make no difference. But warriors used hands and feet. Used weapons. Made attacks.

Gravity's assistance or burden affected every movement. The higher warrior's attack became quick and sharp, the lower warrior's heavy and slow. A large difference in precision followed.

An armor's <ruby>signal scanner<rt>radar</rt></ruby> was the most accurate, quickest means of detection. Only the tiniest delay—the time for the outgoing signal to return—and Muramasa would detect Silver Star's attack beginning.

In the past contests, <ruby>sight<rt>eyes</rt></ruby> was what I had <ruby>relied<rt>relied</rt></ruby> on. And lost.

In range, <ruby>signal scanning<rt>ears</rt></ruby> was unquestionably superior. It would unquestionably get the information before sight.

...But even that would be too late. I knew it.

Probably Muramasa did too.

A grain of delay. A time lag as small as sand. Even that would be fatal. To win, I had to know earlier.

At the very instant Silver Star began attacking...

No. Wrong. <ruby>Even then<rt>・・・・</rt></ruby>, too late.

<ruby>Before it began<rt>・・・・・</rt></ruby>.

Know the moment of attack before the attack happened. Only then could I respond.

To defeat a charge approaching the <ruby>physical limit of speed<rt>velocity of light</rt></ruby>, one way remained.

Go beyond <ruby>time<rt>time</rt></ruby>.

The moment of <ruby>initiative<rt>Sen</rt></ruby>, it was called. In the Yoshino style, the Principle of Darkness.

Nothing that demanded <ruby>so-called<rt>so-called</rt></ruby> supernatural power. What it demanded was observation, fine and painstaking. Build a great tower from small stones—that kind of care.

Not <ruby>seeing<rt>・・</rt></ruby> the attack's movement.

<ruby>Reading<rt>・・</rt></ruby> its signs.

A slight shift of the eyes. Tension in a muscle. From that information, recognize an enemy's attack <ruby>before<rt>・・</rt></ruby> the movement actually began.

Press into that moment and crush the enemy's first move: that was seizing the initiative, the Yoshino style's Principle of Darkness.

Against Silver Star, impossible. Stopping that attack before it began was physically impossible.

After it began, however, an answer was possible. Should be possible.

Read the initiative, then take the <ruby>counter-initiative<rt>Go-no-sen</rt></ruby>—perhaps that was the shape of it. If I could know the dive's arrival even one <ruby>billionth of a second<rt>nanosecond</rt></ruby> sooner, I could <ruby>meet it with my blade<rt>・・・・・・</rt></ruby>.

Perhaps we would kill each other.

But I could bring her down.

　微妙な視線の移動。あるいは筋肉の緊張。
　そういった情報から、敵の攻撃動作が実際に始まる
よりも<ruby>先に<rt>・・</rt></ruby>それを悟る。

できたなら、迎撃の剣を<ruby>合わせられる<rt>・・・・・・</rt></ruby>。

　あるいは相討。
　しかし、斃せる。
